title: Development of Quantum Theory
lead: Bohr’s model could not say why only certain orbits were allowed, and it failed for every atom with more than one electron. In its place came de Broglie’s matter waves, Heisenberg’s limit on knowing position and momentum together, Schrödinger’s wavefunctions, and the four quantum numbers that describe an electron in an atom.
objectives: Extend the concept of wave–particle duality that was observed in electromagnetic radiation to matter as well

Understand the general idea of the quantum mechanical description of electrons in an atom, and that it uses the notion of three-dimensional wave functions, or orbitals, that define the distribution of probability to find an electron in a particular part of space
List and describe traits of the four quantum numbers that form the basis for completely specifying the state of an electron in an atom
summary_html:
Macroscopic objects act as particles. Microscopic objects (such as electrons) have properties of both a particle and a wave. Their exact trajectories cannot be determined. The quantum mechanical model of atoms describes the three-dimensional position of the electron in a probabilistic manner according to a mathematical function called a wavefunction, often denoted as ψ. Atomic wavefunctions are also called orbitals. The squared magnitude of the wavefunction describes the distribution of the probability of finding the electron in a particular region in space. Therefore, atomic orbitals describe the areas in an atom where electrons are most likely to be found.

An atomic orbital is characterized by three quantum numbers. The principal quantum number, n, can be any positive integer. The general region for value of energy of the orbital and the average distance of an electron from the nucleus are related to n. Orbitals having the same value of n are said to be in the same shell. The secondary (angular momentum) quantum number, l, can have any integer value from 0 to n – 1. This quantum number describes the shape or type of the orbital. Orbitals with the same principal quantum number and the same l value belong to the same subshell. The magnetic quantum number, ml, with 2l + 1 values ranging from –l to +l, describes the orientation of the orbital in space. In addition, each electron has a spin quantum number, ms, that can be equal to ±1⁄2. No two electrons in the same atom can have the same set of values for all the four quantum numbers.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the wavelength of a softball with a mass of 100 g traveling at a velocity of 35 m s<sup>–1</sup>, assuming that it can be modeled as a single particle.

answer.hint: Convert the mass to kilograms first, then divide Planck’s constant by the product of mass and velocity.
answer.solution: 1.9 × 10<sup>–34</sup> m. We never think of a thrown softball having a wavelength, since this wavelength is so small it is impossible for our senses or any known instrument to detect. Since de Broglie wavelength is inversely proportional to both particle mass and velocity, the particle’s momentum (mathematical product of mass and velocity) must be sufficiently small to yield a detectably large wavelength.

exercises.prompt: Identify the subshell in which electrons with the following quantum numbers are found: (a) n = 3, l = 1; (b) n = 5, l = 3; (c) n = 2, l = 0.
If a shell contains a maximum of 32 electrons, what is the principal quantum number, n?

answer.hint: A shell with principal quantum number n holds at most 2n² electrons.
A subshell with secondary quantum number l has 2l + 1 orbitals.

exercises.prompt: How are the Bohr model and the quantum mechanical model of the hydrogen atom similar? How are they different?

answer.solution: Both models have a central positively charged nucleus with electrons moving about the nucleus in accordance with the Coulomb electrostatic potential. The Bohr model assumes that the electrons move in circular orbits that have quantized energies, angular momentum, and radii that are specified by a single quantum number, n = 1, 2, 3, …, but this quantization is an ad hoc assumption made by Bohr to incorporate quantization into an essentially classical mechanics description of the atom. Bohr also assumed that electrons orbiting the nucleus normally do not emit or absorb electromagnetic radiation, but do so when the electron switches to a different orbit. In the quantum mechanical model, the electrons do not move in precise orbits (such orbits violate the Heisenberg uncertainty principle) and, instead, a probabilistic interpretation of the electron’s position at any given instant is used, with a mathematical function ψ called a wavefunction that can be used to determine the electron’s spatial probability distribution. These wavefunctions, or orbitals, are three-dimensional stationary waves that can be specified by three quantum numbers that arise naturally from their underlying mathematics (no ad hoc assumptions required): the principal quantum number, n (the same one used by Bohr), which specifies shells such that orbitals having the same n all have the same energy and approximately the same spatial extent; the angular momentum quantum number l, which is a measure of the orbital’s angular momentum and corresponds to the orbitals’ general shapes, as well as specifying subshells such that orbitals having the same l (and n) all have the same energy; and the orientation quantum number m, which is a measure of the z component of the angular momentum and corresponds to the orientations of the orbitals. The Bohr model gives the same expression for the energy as the quantum mechanical expression and, hence, both properly account for hydrogen’s discrete spectrum (an example of getting the right answers for the wrong reasons, something that many chemistry students can sympathize with), but gives the wrong expression for the angular momentum (Bohr orbits necessarily all have non-zero angular momentum, but some quantum orbitals [s orbitals] can have zero angular momentum).

exercises.prompt: What are the allowed values for each of the four quantum numbers: n, l, ml, and ms?

answer.solution: Work down Table 6.1 one row at a time. The principal quantum number n can be any positive integer. The secondary quantum number l depends on n: it takes every integer from 0 up to n – 1. The magnetic quantum number ml depends on l: it takes every integer from –l to +l, which is 2l + 1 values. The spin quantum number ms depends on nothing else and has only two values, +1⁄2 and –1⁄2.

exercises.prompt: Describe the properties of an electron associated with each of the following four quantum numbers: n, l, ml, and ms.

answer.solution: n determines the general range for the value of energy and the probable distances that the electron can be from the nucleus. l determines the shape of the orbital. m1 determines the orientation of the orbitals of the same l value with respect to one another. ms determines the spin of an electron.

exercises.prompt:
Answer the following questions:
(a) Without using quantum numbers, describe the differences between the shells, subshells, and orbitals of an atom.
(b) How do the quantum numbers of the shells, subshells, and orbitals of an atom differ?

answer.solution: (a) Think of the three as nested groups. A shell is the set of orbitals that share one general energy and one general distance from the nucleus. A subshell is the set of orbitals within a shell that share one shape. An orbital is a single region of space, within a subshell, in which one or two electrons are most likely to be found. (b) Ask how many quantum numbers are needed to name each group. A shell is fixed by n alone, a subshell by n and l together, and an orbital by n, l and ml together.

exercises.prompt:
Identify the subshell in which electrons with the following quantum numbers are found:
(a) n = 2, l = 1
(b) n = 4, l = 2
(c) n = 6, l = 0
Which of the subshells described in the previous question contain degenerate orbitals? How many degenerate orbitals are in each?

answer.solution: Degenerate orbitals are orbitals of the same energy, and the orbitals of one subshell are degenerate with one another. A subshell with secondary quantum number l holds 2l + 1 orbitals, one for each value of ml, so a subshell contains degenerate orbitals only when 2l + 1 is greater than one. Read l for each of the three subshells and count 2l + 1 for each.

exercises.prompt:
Identify the subshell in which electrons with the following quantum numbers are found:
(a) n = 3, l = 2
(b) n = 1, l = 0
(c) n = 4, l = 3
Which of the subshells described in the previous question contain degenerate orbitals? How many degenerate orbitals are in each?

answer.solution: Orbitals in one subshell share one energy, so they are degenerate. Read the value of l from the letter of each subshell (s for 0, p for 1, d for 2, f for 3) and count the 2l + 1 values of ml that it allows; a subshell with only one orbital has no other orbital to be degenerate with.

exercises.prompt: Sketch the boundary surface of a $d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}$ and a py orbital. Be sure to show and label the axes.
Sketch the px and dxz orbitals. Be sure to show and label the coordinates.

answer.solution: Draw the x, y and z axes first, with the nucleus at the origin. A p orbital is a dumbbell of two lobes that lies along the axis named in its subscript, so the px orbital has one lobe on each side of the origin along the x axis. A d orbital with two letters in its subscript has four lobes in the plane of those two axes, lying between the axes rather than along them, so the dxz orbital has four lobes in the xz plane, one in each quarter of it. Figure 6.21 shows both shapes and can be turned to check the sketch.

exercises.prompt:
Consider the orbitals shown here in outline.
(a) What is the maximum number of electrons contained in an orbital of type (x)? Of type (y)? Of type (z)?
(b) How many orbitals of type (x) are found in a shell with n = 2? How many of type (y)? How many of type (z)?
(c) Write a set of quantum numbers for an electron in an orbital of type (x) in a shell with n = 4. Of an orbital of type (y) in a shell with n = 2. Of an orbital of type (z) in a shell with n = 3.
(d) What is the smallest possible n value for an orbital of type (x)? Of type (y)? Of type (z)?
(e) What are the possible l and ml values for an orbital of type (x)? Of type (y)? Of type (z)?

answer.solution: (a) x. 2, y. 2, z. 2; (b) x. 1, y. 3, z. 0; (c) x. 4 0 0 1⁄2, y. 2 1 0 1⁄2, z. 3 2 0 1⁄2; (d) x. 1, y. 2, z. 3; (e) x. l = 0, ml = 0, y. l = 1, ml = –1, 0, or +1, z. l = 2, ml = –2, –1, 0, +1, +2

exercises.prompt: State the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. Describe briefly what the principle implies.

answer.solution: Start from the principle: it is fundamentally impossible to determine simultaneously and exactly both the momentum and the position of a particle. The product of the two uncertainties, Δx × Δpx, can be no smaller than ħ/2. Then say what follows. The more exactly we know the position of a particle, the less exactly we can know its momentum. An electron in an atom therefore cannot be followed along a precise orbit, as the Bohr model supposed, and its position can only be described by a probability. Because ħ is so small, the limit matters for a particle as light as an electron but is far too small to notice for a macroscopic object such as a baseball.

exercises.prompt: How many electrons could be held in the second shell of an atom if the spin quantum number ms could have three values instead of just two? (Hint: Consider the Pauli exclusion principle.)

answer.hint: Count the orbitals of the second shell, then ask how many electrons one orbital could hold if no two could share all four quantum numbers.

exercises.prompt:
Which of the following equations describe particle-like behavior? Which describe wavelike behavior? Do any involve both types of behavior? Describe the reasons for your choices.
(a) c = λν
(b) $E=\frac{m{\nu}^{2}}{2}$
(c) $r=\frac{{n}^{2}{a}_{0}}{Z}$
(d) E = hν
(e) $\lambda=\frac{h}{m\nu}$

answer.solution: Sort each equation by the quantities it contains. A wavelength λ or a frequency ν belongs to a wave, while a mass m, a speed or a definite radius belongs to a particle. An equation that holds only wave quantities describes wavelike behavior, one that holds only particle quantities describes particle-like behavior, and one that sets a wave quantity equal to an expression in particle quantities joins the two. Note that in (b) and (e) the book writes the velocity of the particle with the same letter it uses for frequency, so read that symbol as a velocity there, as in de Broglie’s equation.
